result.summary: A Mouse laments the loss of three sons to the Frogs' side and persuades the Mice to arm. The Frogs arm in turn after a herald's challenge, the gods decline to take sides, and the first fighting begins.

scenes.title: The Mice arm for war
scenes.summary: A bereaved Mouse recounts the deaths of his three sons and urges war. The Mice are armed with comic gear made of household scraps.
scenes.stakes: The Mice risk open war with the Frogs to avenge their dead kin.

place.name: the Mice's land by the lake

scenes.title: The Frogs answer and arm
scenes.summary: The Frogs hold a council, hear the herald's challenge, and Puff-jaw denies guilt. He proposes a plan and the Frogs arm with leaves and shells.
scenes.stakes: Puff-jaw is blamed for a death and the Frogs face attack.

scenes.title: The gods refuse to intervene
scenes.summary: Zeus asks which gods will help each side. Athena refuses both, citing grievances, and the gods decide to watch as war is sounded.
scenes.stakes: Gods risk being wounded if they join the fighting.

scenes.title: The first battle
scenes.summary: Frogs and Mice trade blows and many fall, the lake running red.
scenes.stakes: The warriors risk death in battle.

notable_quotes.reason: Athena's comic complaint about borrowing money and owing interest.

analysis.text: The poem parodies Homeric epic by giving tiny animals heroic arming scenes, councils and divine spectators.
The gods' petty grievances mock traditional epic religion and everyday concerns like debt and noise.

legacy.text: The Batrachomyomachia became a model of mock-epic, influencing later works such as Pope's The Rape of the Lock.

fun_facts.text: The poem was anciently attributed to Homer, though scholars generally regard it as a later parody.

language_notes.text: 'First essay at mischief' means the first attempt or sample of harm; the Mouse argues the Frogs' wrongs will continue against all Mice.
'Unheard-of arts' means devices never known before; the Mouse sees the trap as a strange, wicked human invention.
Greaves are armour for the shins, here comically made from gnawed bean-pods.
The 'centre-piece of a lamp' is the boss, the middle part of a lamp, used as a small round shield.
A wand here is a herald's staff, the sign of a messenger's protected status.
'Dry-hobs' is the translator's rendering of a mocking name for the Mice, who live on dry land.
A trophy was a monument of captured arms set up on the battlefield to mark victory.
Centaurs and Giants were mythic races famed for violent battle with gods and heroes; the comparison grandly inflates the tiny animal armies.
"Mischief" here means damage or harm; the mice are treated as pests who spoil her offerings.
The sacred robe (peplos) was woven for Athena's statue and presented at the Panathenaic festival in Athens.
Athena jokes that she, a goddess, is dunned by a money-lender; "interest" on a debt is bitter even for immortals.
"Not considerable" means not worthy of regard; she dismisses the Frogs as unimportant and annoying.
"Fell" means cruel or deadly; the gnats' trumpets are a mock-heroic touch.
Troglodyte means "cave-dweller"; the warriors' names describe animal habits, like Lickman and Bread-nibbler.

context_notes.text: Ares was the Greek god of war. Here he serves as the mock-heroic armourer of the Mice.
The names are comic: Pot-visitor and Cheese-carver describe mouse habits, parodying Homeric heralds and fathers' names.
The Frogs' armour is made of marsh and garden plants, matching their habitat as the Mice's gear matches the household.
Zeus is called son of Cronos, a Titan he overthrew; this patronymic is a standard Homeric formula.
Athena, goddess of wisdom, war and weaving, had a temple at Athens where offerings of oil and food were made.
Zeus's thunder is the traditional divine sign that battle begins, as in Homer's Iliad.

literary_notes.text: The Mice's breastplates come from a ferret, the very enemy that killed a son, making vengeance part of their gear.
Epic arming-scene conventions, even 'the work of Ares', are applied to lamp parts, needles and nutshells, creating humour.
Calling the challenge 'blameless speech' is ironic, since it accuses the Frogs of a killing their king denies.
Puff-jaw's glib excuse shows him evasive and self-serving, shifting blame onto the drowned Mouse's foolish play.
Tiny creatures are described with epic grandeur, comparing them to Giants and Centaurs, for comic effect.
Zeus's sly smile shows he treats the war as amusement, undercutting the epic solemnity of the gathering.
Athena's petty complaints about holes in her robe and debts mock the lofty divine councils of Homeric epic.
The fall, the clashing armour and the dust imitate Iliad death scenes, applied absurdly to a mouse.
The lake dyed with red blood gives a vivid, Iliad-like picture of slaughter, set in a pond.
